title: Life-Insurers' Appetite for Super-Long JGBs: What It Means for the Market
abstract: A careful look at what Japanese life insurers actually said about super-long JGBs this month, and what the market did with it.
body:
On 2026-07-20, I spent the morning rereading the quarterly investment plans that Japan's nine largest life insurers published over the past two weeks. I do this every quarter, partly out of habit from my years on the buy-side desk at the Bank of Japan, and partly because the life insurers remain the single most important marginal buyer of super-long JGBs. What they say about duration is often more informative than what the BoJ says about yield curve control, because the insurers are the ones who actually have to put money to work.

This quarter's plans were notable for their caution. Seven of the nine insurers said they would keep their yen duration roughly unchanged in the fiscal year ending March 2027. Two said they would modestly extend duration, but only if the 30-year yield rose above a level they did not specify. None said they would shorten duration. That is a subtle but important shift from a year ago, when three insurers explicitly flagged that they were underweight super-long JGBs relative to their liability benchmarks.

## What the insurers actually said

The headline numbers were not dramatic. The nine insurers collectively plan to buy about 2.1 trillion yen of super-long JGBs in the current fiscal year, down from 2.8 trillion yen in the previous year. That sounds bearish, but the decline is mostly mechanical: redemptions of existing holdings are lower this year, so gross purchases can fall without net purchases falling. On a net basis, the insurers expect to add roughly 900 billion yen of duration, which is close to the average of the past five years.

The more interesting signal was in the language. Several insurers used the phrase "waiting for clarity" when describing their stance on the 30-year and 40-year sectors. In my experience, that phrase usually means the insurers think yields are too low relative to their long-term expectations, but they are unwilling to say so publicly because they do not want to be seen as talking their book. It is a polite way of saying they are not buyers at current levels.

One insurer, which I will not name because the disclosure is buried in a footnote, said it had shifted part of its super-long allocation into foreign bonds, specifically US Treasuries and Australian government bonds, on a hedged basis. That is a meaningful change. For most of the past decade, Japanese life insurers have treated super-long JGBs as the default asset for matching long-dated liabilities. If they are now willing to look abroad, even on a hedged basis, it tells you something about their view of relative value.

## What the market did

The market reaction was muted, which I found more revealing than the plans themselves. The 30-year JGB yield rose by about 3 basis points in the two days after the largest insurers published, from 2.41% to 2.44%. The 40-year yield rose by a similar amount. The 20-year yield was essentially unchanged. For a market that is often described as fragile, that is a remarkably calm response to news that the largest buyer is stepping back.

I think there are three reasons for the calm. First, the insurers' plans were widely expected. The sell-side had been forecasting a decline in gross purchases for weeks. Second, the BoJ's own purchases have been more predictable this year, which has reduced the tail risk of a sudden supply-demand mismatch. Third, and most importantly, the regional banks and the Government Pension Investment Fund have been more active in the super-long sector, filling part of the gap left by the insurers.

That last point deserves more attention than it has received. The GPIF does not publish its quarterly JGB purchase plans in the same way the insurers do, but its flow data suggest it has been a net buyer of super-long JGBs for three consecutive quarters. If that continues, the insurers' caution may not translate into higher yields at all. It may simply mean a rotation of ownership within the domestic investor base.

## The BoJ angle

The Bank of Japan's policy stance remains the dominant factor for super-long yields, and here I want to be careful about what we know versus what we infer. At the June 2026 meeting, the BoJ kept its policy rate unchanged and made no change to its JGB purchase plan. The statement said the bank would "continue to monitor developments in financial markets" — a phrase that has appeared in every statement since 2024 and therefore carries little information.

What we can infer from the minutes, which were released on 2026-07-10, is that the board discussed the super-long sector explicitly. One member noted that "the functioning of the super-long market has improved" since the bank reduced its purchases in that sector last year. Another member cautioned that "a further reduction should be considered carefully." That is not a policy signal, but it does suggest the board is not in a hurry to change its purchase schedule.

For life insurers, that matters because it reduces the risk of a sudden spike in yields. If the BoJ is on hold, the insurers can afford to wait. If the BoJ were to surprise with a faster taper, the insurers would likely be forced to buy more aggressively to match their liabilities, which would put downward pressure on yields. The asymmetry is important: the insurers' caution is conditional on BoJ predictability.

## What I am watching next

I am watching three things over the next quarter. First, the insurers' mid-year revisions, which usually come out in October. If the two insurers that said they might extend duration actually do so, that would be a meaningful signal. Second, the GPIF's next flow report, due in early August. If the GPIF continues to buy super-long JGBs, the market can absorb the insurers' caution without much difficulty. Third, the BoJ's September meeting, where the board will update its economic projections. If the projections show higher long-term inflation expectations, the insurers may feel more pressure to extend duration, not less.

I should be clear about what I am not saying. I am not saying the insurers are bearish on JGBs. I am not saying yields are about to rise sharply. I am saying that the marginal buyer of super-long JGBs is becoming more selective, and that the market has so far taken that in stride. That is a healthier outcome than the alternative, but it also means the super-long sector is more dependent on a narrower set of buyers than it was a year ago. For a market that is still adjusting to the end of yield curve control, that is worth keeping an eye on.
